reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

summary: Fraud detection and credit modelling are decades old; generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in Finance and insurance (NAICS 52) at 41.0% of firms, up from 36.5% in the prior period, based on firms answering yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks. The survey first asked the question in September 2023. That figure covers the whole finance and insurance sector rather than banking alone, so it is a ceiling and a context line rather than a bank-specific number.

What the technology is used for splits by vintage. According to this site's coverage of the sector, fraud detection and credit models are decades old, while generative AI in service and compliance is the new frontier. The Financial Models section on this site tracks the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, downloads and release date, refreshed daily, drawing on the Hugging Face Hub public API sorted by all-time downloads, and describes those models as tuned for financial text.

Evident Insights runs the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard. Its Evident AI Index benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services and scores the major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics covering talent, innovation, leadership and transparency. The index launched in January 2023, the 2026 Evident AI Index for Banks returns in October, and Evident has extended the work to regional bank indices for Latin America and the Middle East and Africa plus a separate index for insurance. Evident's own framing is that several of the world's biggest banks have quietly become AI-powered behemoths and that banks are among the businesses racing to incorporate the technology into almost everything they do. Its Banking Brief newsletter reports over 15,000 subscribers across banking, tech, consulting, academia and government. The material here contains no dollar figures on where vendor spending concentrates, so nothing can be said about that.

On returns, these sources are largely silent for banking. The only adjacent signal is Evident's description of its insurance index, which it says explores where the technology is starting to unlock value and where insurers should focus next. No quantified ROI figures for banks appear in the material provided.

The regulatory posture is the sector's distinguishing feature. Per this site's curated points, credit and AML models operate under the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, which makes banking the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade, and the letter is listed in the Fed's 2011 supervisory letters index. The Fed page cited here is that index, and the excerpt shown is a different 2011 letter on dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies. The site's curated point also describes a Treasury report on AI in financial services, covering uses, opportunities and risks, that frames the US supervisory conversation, but the Treasury page cited is a sanctions press release about a gold smuggling and money laundering network, in which OFAC sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses under Executive Order 13818. That page does not itself document AI use in banking.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow set of conclusions. Adoption is substantial and rising, at 41.0% across finance and insurance, but it is not universal, and the Census figure is not bank-specific. Public benchmarking exists through the Evident AI Index if you want to see how large banks compare on talent, innovation, leadership and transparency. Governance is not a blank slate, since model risk management expectations have applied to credit and AML models since 2011. What the sources do not provide is evidence on returns, so any ROI case has to come from your own deployment rather than from this material.

https://evidentinsights.com/.brief: Evident Insights is an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across the financial services sector. It supplies data, research, and benchmarking to help financial services leaders make informed AI-related decisions, investments, and strategic choices. The platform publishes the Evident AI Index, which ranks banks and insurers on their AI deployment and highlights emerging trends. Since launching in January 2023, the index has sparked debate and received widespread press coverage, with Evident CEO Alexandra Mousavizadeh frequently commenting on global AI trends.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page catalogues the 1,000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, according to The World of AI. It lists each model’s licence, download count, and release date, and the collection is refreshed daily. The data is drawn from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, and every model links to its own Hub page. The page was last verified on 2026-09-25.
